references.text: Cain lured his brother Abel out into the field and killed him—the first example of fratricide motivated by jealousy, a parallel to Joseph's brothers who planned to kill him.
Esau planned to kill his brother Jacob because of the blessing he had taken, a direct parallel to brothers plotting murder out of jealousy.
Saul spoke with Jonathan and his servants about killing David—a parallel to Joseph's brothers who conspired to take his life.
Jeremiah describes how his enemies plotted evil against him without his knowledge, a strong parallel to Joseph's brothers who planned against him as he approached.

In the parable of the wicked tenants, the leaseholders see the son coming and plan to kill him to seize the inheritance—a typological parallel to Joseph's brothers who saw him from afar and plotted to kill him.
Pilate knew it was out of envy (jealousy) that they had handed over Jesus, a parallel to the brothers' jealousy that motivated their murder plots against Joseph.
More than forty Jews took an oath to kill Paul and made a plan to carry it out—a parallel to the brothers' conspiracy against Joseph.
Clear typological parallel: Joseph as a forerunner of Jesus, where both become the object of conspiracies to be killed by their own people.
Thematic parallel: Conspiracy against the innocent (Joseph vs. Jesus) carried out by their own brothers or community.
Direct narrative connection: Refers back to Joseph himself and his suffering (archers) as a summary of the brothers' attack.
Thematic parallel: Religious leaders conspire against the righteous (Joseph's brothers vs. the Pharisees).
Thematic parallel: Religious authorities plot to kill God's chosen one (Joseph's brothers vs. the chief priests).
Narrative parallel: Use of deceit in the conspiracy against the righteous (Joseph and Jesus).
